what_it_does: When an AI chip runs a neural network, it breaks the work into many small matrix operations — essentially large grids of numbers being multiplied together — and shuttles data between the chip's fast on-chip memory and slower off-chip memory. Figuring out the best order and layout (called a 'dataflow') for these operations is a huge search problem, and most tools just guess or search blindly. This paper derives mathematical principles that tell you the minimum amount of data movement any dataflow must do for a given operation, giving designers a hard lower bound to target. It also works out these bounds for 'fused' operators — where two back-to-back operations are merged to avoid writing intermediate results to memory — and proposes an architecture called FuseCU that can exploit profitable fusions. The value is turning a search problem into a principled design guide, though the practical speedups on real chips are not confirmed from the abstract alone.
